subtype: Approach: planning what to do if she forgets a line [Thinking]
passage: I'm Omkar, and I was in the audience during rehearsal when Parveen stopped mid-scene, looking worried. She turned to the teacher afterwards. "What if I forget my line on the day?" The teacher did not say 'you won't'. Instead they sat on the stage steps and made a plan together. If Parveen forgets, she pauses, takes a slow breath, and looks at Tara, who says the next line. Parveen repeated it twice, then practised it, even pretending to forget a line so she could try the pause. During the show she did forget, once, and it worked: the pause was so short that most people never noticed.

qa.q: Who says the next line if Parveen forgets?
What was Parveen worried about after the rehearsal?
qa.a: Parveen worried about forgetting her line on the day, and wanted a plan for it.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Parveen use as well, and why?
qa.a: Parveen could keep a small cue word in mind or practise the line with friends until it is automatic. More than one safety net gives even more calm.

qa.q: How does Omkar see the plan?
qa.a: Omkar watched from the audience and saw the pause work, so Omkar probably feels impressed by how a small plan kept the show moving.

grounding: A girl asks what if she forgets and plans with her teacher to pause, breathe and look at Tara who has the next line, seen by an observer.

subtype: Approach: planning what to do if she forgets a line [Thinking]
passage:
Monday: At rehearsal Nazia froze on her third line, and the play stopped. Afterwards she asked the teacher, "What if I forget on the day?"
Wednesday: They sat together with the script. "If it goes, what will you do?" the teacher asked. Nazia thought. "Stop. Breathe. Then look at Chaitanya, because he has the next line." "And?" "He can say it, or give me my first word." They told Chaitanya. He grinned. "I'll be your backup."
Saturday: On stage, Nazia's second line vanished. She paused, took a breath, and looked at Chaitanya. He whispered, "The river..." She picked it up. The audience never knew.

qa.q: Who has the line after Nazia's?
How did Nazia feel after freezing on Monday?
qa.a: She felt worried about forgetting on the day, which is why she asked the teacher what to do.

qa.q: What else could Nazia add to her plan, and why?
qa.a: She could keep a tiny script inside a prop, because a second backup helps if Chaitanya is also flustered.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Chaitanya?
qa.a: Chaitanya is happy to be her backup, grinning, and feels trusted with an important job.

grounding: It shows a child who fears forgetting a line planning with her teacher to pause, breathe and look at the friend with the next line.

subtype: Approach: planning what to do if she forgets a line [Thinking]
passage: Himani, you're scared you'll forget your lines in the play? Listen to your Sangeeta Nani. When I was small, in our school in Shimla, I played the rabbit in a forest play. I was sure I would forget. I asked my teacher, "What if my mind goes blank?" She didn't say "you won't." She said, "Then what will you do?" We made a plan. Stop. Take one breath. Look at the squirrel, my friend Kamla, who had the line after mine. On the day, it happened. Halfway through, blank. I stopped. Breathed. Looked at Kamla. She mouthed "carrots", and it all came back. People only saw a rabbit thinking.

qa.q: What part did Sangeeta play in the forest play?
How did young Sangeeta feel before the play?
qa.a: She was scared and sure she would forget her lines.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Asking "what if" and making a plan made the difference, because when the blank came there was already a step ready.

qa.q: How might Kamla have felt when Sangeeta looked at her?
qa.a: Kamla probably felt a quick rush of nerves and then pride at helping by mouthing "carrots".

grounding: An elder recalls planning with a teacher, as a young girl, to pause, breathe and look at the friend with the next line, so a slip did not stop the show.
